claims.text: Atomic-scale lattice distortion arising from atomic size mismatch is the primary control on strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion enhances yield strength.
Lattice distortion affects deformation and failure pathways.
Substitution with chemically similar elements having significantly different atomic radii will increase lattice distortion.
The proposed substitutions can vary atomic size mismatch while keeping electron concentration and valence approximately constant.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening analysis or high-resolution TEM can quantify nanometer-scale local lattice distortions.
Increased atomic size mismatch produces enhanced local lattice distortion.
Enhanced local lattice distortion generates internal stress fields.
Distortion-induced internal stress fields interact with moving dislocations.
The interaction between internal stress fields and dislocations raises the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
A higher barrier to dislocation motion increases alloy strength.
Altered dislocation dynamics can affect ductility and the eventual failure mode.
Under identical test conditions, the higher-distortion alloy will exhibit higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The higher-distortion alloy may exhibit a dislocation density or distribution distinct from that of the baseline alloy.
The proposed effect should hold in homogeneous, fully solid-solution microstructures without significant grain-boundary or precipitate strengthening contributions.
Short-range atomic order, segregation, and alloy-specific competing strengthening mechanisms may alter the magnitude of the proposed effect.
A failure to observe significantly increased yield strength and altered dislocation behavior in the higher-mismatch alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experimental design require substitution of different elements to alter atomic-radius mismatch, whereas the baseline is described as identical in composition. Elemental substitution necessarily changes composition, so the proposed samples cannot be both compositionally identical and different in substituted elements.
